title: Chemically complete atomic structures of bulk amorphous solids

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to experimentally determine where the atoms are, and which elements they are, throughout a volume of an amorphous solid that represents the bulk material. The target includes chemically complex materials such as oxide glasses, polymers and glassy electrolytes, with oxygen or other light elements resolved alongside heavier atoms. The resulting three-dimensional atomic model would be validated against measurements withheld from its construction and refinement.

An ideal periodic crystal can be described by a finite atomic basis and repeating symmetry. An amorphous solid lacks that repeating description, but it can still be represented by atomic coordinates; experimental examples already exist for particular metallic specimens. The advance sought here is a chemically complete, independently validated description of a representative volume, extending beyond those demonstrations. Pair-distribution functions summarize separations between pairs of atoms and do not, by themselves, uniquely determine the full three-dimensional arrangement.

significance.text: Reliable coordinates and chemical identities would allow competing descriptions of short- and medium-range order to be tested directly. Researchers could examine which atoms surround each site, how structural motifs connect, and whether proposed chemical ordering actually occurs. Existing metallic-material studies demonstrate the value of this approach: the 2021 multi-component alloy study identified four types of crystal-like medium-range order. Extending comparable analysis to representative light-element covalent networks would substantially broaden the materials accessible to direct atomic structure determination.

Impact synthesis: the comparison with Bragg crystallography concerns the enabling power of experimentally grounded structural knowledge. It does not imply that a sampled glass configuration plays the same role as a repeating crystal unit cell. Different regions and independently prepared specimens can have different atomic arrangements while sharing bulk properties. Conditional on representative sampling and reliable chemistry, coordinate sets could help connect network structure to mechanical behavior, electronic properties or ion transport, but coordinates alone would not establish those causal relationships or guarantee predictive materials design.

Scope synthesis: a liquid introduces an additional challenge because its arrangement changes with time. An experimentally resolved ultrafast snapshot would describe a particular configuration, while a representative liquid ensemble would require adequate temporal or statistical sampling. Neither capability follows automatically from reconstructing a static amorphous solid.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is joint recovery of atomic positions and element identities in chemically complex, bulk-representative amorphous specimens, with quantified errors and independent experimental validation. Detecting an atomic peak is not equivalent to identifying its element. The January 2026 simulation analysis finds that chemical discrimination depends on noise, experimental sampling, composition and background: overlapping intensity distributions can leave substantial ambiguity, particularly for lighter atoms.

The engineering barriers interact. Electron fluence must provide sufficient information while avoiding beam-induced movement, structural transformation or damage. Specimen thickness and depth of focus constrain imaging; incomplete angular coverage creates a missing wedge; sampling and registration errors affect reconstruction. The retained 2026 supplement describes its information requirement estimate as optimistic and excludes missing-wedge effects, beam-induced changes and registration errors from that estimate. A favorable calculation therefore does not establish achievable performance under all experimental conditions.

Open research question: whether every atom in a thick, multi-element glass can be located and chemically identified at a tolerable dose remains quantitatively unresolved in the supplied evidence. Bulk representativeness adds a separate requirement: an accurately reconstructed small region may still omit important structural variation. The supplied record establishes these challenges, but does not establish that the broader target remains unachieved across all relevant materials as of November 1, 2026.

current_state.text: Yang and colleagues reported experimental three-dimensional atomic coordinates for a multi-component glass-forming alloy in Nature on March 31, 2021. Their coordinate-based analysis identified four types of crystal-like medium-range order. This is an experimental demonstration of structural analysis in an amorphous metallic material. The supplied research describes a nanoparticle, but the retained PubMed abstract does not independently establish its dimensions, complete element resolution or independently verified reconstruction accuracy.

Yuan and colleagues, in a Nature Materials study published online on October 18, 2021, reported three-dimensional atomic positions for a monatomic amorphous Ta thin film and two Pd nanoparticles. The Ta specimen was a thin film, so the achievements cannot accurately be summarized as nanoparticles alone. These monatomic results establish positional structure determination in their tested specimens; they do not by themselves demonstrate chemical identification in a multi-element oxide, polymer or electrolyte glass.

Busch, Rez, Treacy and Zuo published a simulation analysis in Nature on January 28, 2026 examining when atomic electron tomography can identify all or most atoms in amorphous nanoparticles. The reported limitations are conditional: positional and chemical accuracy depend on fluence, sampling, composition, background and other experimental conditions. Heavier atoms are easier to resolve, and overlapping atomic-peak and background intensities can produce large chemical-identification uncertainties. These findings do not establish that amorphous tomography generally fails.

The retained peer-review exchange for the 2026 analysis records substantive disagreement over simulation realism and reconstruction accuracy, including competing estimates and concerns that simulations omitted experimental error sources. This exchange contextualizes the published simulation findings; it is not a settled experimental determination of universal accuracy or impossibility. The supplied review had access to a partial subscription preview, a complete retained supplement and a partially available peer-review file with explicit redactions. Referenced attachments and figure images were not inspected.

The supplied research also attributes a million-atom reconstruction of simulated model particles to a Science Bulletin article dated January 15, 2025, volume 70, pages 64–69, together with a description of conventional atomic tomography as mainly limited to specimens below 10 nm. No source artifact was retained for that citation, so those numerical and scope claims remain unverified here. Even if confirmed, reconstruction of simulated particles would establish computational performance under the tested assumptions, rather than experimental chemical completeness in a bulk-representative glass. Missing evidence does not establish that the report is false.

The evidence base is narrower than a comprehensive assessment through November 1, 2026. The retained 2021 records provide abstracts or subscription previews rather than complete main articles; the Yuan supplement contributes additional methodological text, but its figure pixels were not inspected. The supplied freshness search record is empty. Consequently, the documented advances can be described, but the absence of a later validated bulk covalent or molecular glass result cannot be established from these inputs.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: experimentally locate and chemically identify at least 95 percent of atoms in an amorphous specimen that includes oxygen or another light element and extends beyond a sub-10-nanometer metal-rich particle. Report atom recovery and chemical-identification accuracy separately for each element, together with false positives, missed atoms, ambiguous assignments and coordinate uncertainty. The 95 percent threshold and specimen exclusion are proposed benchmarks, not established community standards; 95 percent recovery would not constitute literal chemical completeness.
completion_criteria.label: Locate and chemically identify ≥95% of atoms, including light elements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed representativeness test: establish agreement with independent composition, density and structural measurements appropriate to the material, and assess whether the sampled volume captures relevant structural variation. Composition alone is insufficient because different atomic networks can share the same elemental proportions. A network fitted only to a pair-distribution function would not meet the target of experimentally determined, independently validated atomic coordinates.
completion_criteria.label: Show representative atomic networks agreeing with independent bulk measurements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and validation package: publish atomic coordinates, chemical assignments, raw projections, acquisition conditions and reconstruction methods, and obtain a blinded independent reconstruction. Reconstructing the same projections independently tests reproducibility; validating against measurements withheld from both reconstruction and refinement tests a different requirement. The Yuan supplement describes simulated images generated from its recovered atomic model for a precision check. Such model-derived checks can test internal consistency, but do not substitute for independent experimental measurements.
completion_criteria.label: Publish atomic data with blinded reconstruction and withheld experimental validation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: document the demonstrated ranges of thickness, dose, composition, chemical contrast and beam sensitivity, including evidence that acquisition preserved the structure being measured. Repeat the result across independent specimens and, for broader claims, across distinct material classes. Success in one oxide, polymer or electrolyte glass would establish capability for that tested case. Finite demonstrations establish breadth within tested conditions, not universal applicability to amorphous matter.
completion_criteria.label: Document reproducible operating limits and evidence acquisition preserves structure

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CRX-04, “Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering,” overlaps strongly in its concern with disordered atomic structure. Its stated target is an ensemble inferred from total scattering; CRX-02 targets experimentally localized atoms and their chemical identities within representative amorphous volumes. Ensemble information and localized coordinates could be complementary, but neither target should be treated as automatically satisfying the other.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-01, “Atomic-resolution imaging of a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction,” shares the difficulties of imaging without periodic repetition and preserving information under destructive exposure. Its object is an individual molecule, whereas CRX-02 concerns a representative volume of an extended solid. CRX-08, “Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once,” overlaps in recovering structure without repeatable copies, but uniqueness of the specimen is not a defining requirement of CRX-02.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-09, “Protonation state as a routine crystallographic observable,” intersects with the challenge of assigning light elements and chemical states. Element identity and atomic position alone do not necessarily determine protonation state. CRX-12, concerning continuous atomic-resolution crystallography in working devices and static extreme environments, adds operational and environmental requirements beyond the static structural target here. CRX-06, concerning atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger, adds temporal resolution; a static amorphous reconstruction is not an atomic movie.

Roster-based comparison: CRX-13, “A growth rulebook that suppresses defects, twins, and disorder in arbitrary crystals,” concerns controlling structure during crystal growth. CRX-02 concerns measuring an existing amorphous structure. Both address disorder, but their central outcomes are distinct. The supplied roster supports this title-level distinction; fuller boundaries would require the detailed CRX-13 definition. The earlier mapping to historical item 6 cannot be checked because that item's definition was not supplied.

unresolved_issues: Whether the broader target remained unachieved as of November 1, 2026 cannot be established without a populated freshness record.
The 2025 Science Bulletin million-atom simulation report, its bibliographic details and the associated below-10-nanometer scope claim lack a retained source artifact.
The tolerable-dose feasibility of locating and chemically identifying every atom in a thick, multi-element glass remains quantitatively unresolved.
The supplied partial records do not establish the multi-component alloy specimen's dimensions, complete element resolution or independently verified accuracy.
Disagreement over simulation realism and accuracy in the 2026 peer-review exchange remains unresolved; redactions, uninspected attachments and uninspected figure images limit interpretation.
The proposed completeness threshold requires an operational method for estimating total atom counts and per-element errors without circular reliance on the reconstructed model.
Material-specific representative-volume requirements and practical limits across oxides, polymers and electrolyte glasses remain to be demonstrated.
Historical item 6 was not supplied. Related-concept comparisons rely on roster titles rather than complete definitions; the CRX-13 title supports the broad distinction but not a full scope mapping.

brief.title: Mapping every atom inside glass and plastics
possible: Researchers could see where each atom sits and which element it is inside glass, plastics and other solids whose atoms lack a repeating pattern. The map would cover enough material to represent its internal structure, including light elements such as oxygen.
why: Researchers could directly test competing ideas about how atoms connect in these materials. They could examine each atom’s neighbours and trace how small groups join into larger networks.
These maps could help researchers connect internal structure to how materials bend, conduct electricity or let ions—electrically charged atoms—move through them.

sources.showed: They mapped atom positions in a metal mixture without a repeating atomic pattern. They found crystal-like arrangements extending beyond neighbouring atoms.
sources.quote: Using a multi-component glass-forming alloy as proof of principle, we quantitatively characterize the short- and medium-range order of the 3D atomic arrangement.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates experimental mapping and structural analysis in a disordered metal.
sources.not_established: It does not establish complete element identification in a volume representative of a chemically complex glass.

sources.showed: They used electron tomography, which builds spatial maps from electron images, to locate atoms in a tantalum film and palladium particles. Each specimen contained a single element.
sources.quote: Here we use atomic electron tomography to experimentally determine the three-dimensional atomic positions of monatomic amorphous solids, namely a Ta thin film and two Pd nanoparticles.
sources.cited_for: Atomic positions have been measured in disordered metal films as well as particles.
sources.not_established: Single-element specimens do not test whether different elements can be reliably distinguished in a complex glass.

sources.who: Robert Busch, Peter Rez, Michael M. J. Treacy and Jian-Min Zuo
sources.showed: Their simulations found that atom locations and element identities depend on image noise and measurement conditions. Heavy atoms were easier to distinguish than light atoms.
sources.quote: Heavier atoms are more easily resolved than lighter ones, and large chemical analysis uncertainties emerge when atomic peak and background intensities overlap.
sources.cited_for: Locating an atom does not guarantee that its element can be identified.
sources.not_established: Simulations do not establish achievable accuracy in real specimens or a universal limit on the method.

sources.showed: This is a computational study of reconstructing simulated particles containing a million atoms.
sources.cited_for: The work concerns reconstruction at larger computational scales.
sources.not_established: Simulated particles do not demonstrate experimental identification of every atom in a representative glass.

shown: Yang and colleagues mapped atomic positions in a disordered metal mixture and found crystal-like arrangements within it. Yuan and colleagues mapped positions in a tantalum film and palladium particles. These demonstrations establish that disordered metal specimens can be mapped atom by atom.
missing: The target requires both positions and element identities, including light elements, with measured errors in chemically complex specimens.
Mapped regions must capture the material’s structural variation and agree with independent measurements.
Independent teams must reproduce the maps, which must also pass experimental checks excluded from their construction.
Measurements must preserve the structure while collecting enough information to distinguish atoms.

milestones.label: Positions and elements identified for at least 95% of atoms
milestones.explanation: An experiment would have to meet this target, including light elements, beyond tiny metal-rich particles, with errors measured separately for each element. This would test whether chemical mapping extends beyond metal demonstrations.

milestones.label: Representative atomic networks match independent bulk measurements
milestones.explanation: Mapped networks would have to capture structural variation and agree with independent composition, density and structure measurements. This would connect the sampled region to the material as a whole.

milestones.label: Published data pass blinded reconstruction and independent validation
milestones.explanation: Published atom maps, raw images, acquisition details and methods would have to pass blinded independent reconstruction and checks withheld from building or refining the maps. This would test reproducibility and accuracy separately.

milestones.label: Repeatable operating limits preserve the measured structure
milestones.explanation: Repeated experiments would have to establish workable thickness, exposure and composition ranges while showing that imaging preserves structure. Tests across specimens and material classes would establish the capability’s practical reach.

uncertain: Can enough information be collected to identify every atom in a thick, mixed-element glass without changing its structure?
How can total atom counts and errors be estimated without assuming the reconstructed map is correct?
How large a region must be mapped to represent each material’s structural variation?
